method.fit_population: One vote per exact-text hash and maximum 9 fit votes per normalized filer field
method.all_filing_scoring: Every filing transformed against the same topic model; nonexclusive topic membership at >=42% of its maximum topic score
method.candidate_selection: No preselected advocacy sentence filter or fixed regulatory keywords. All extracted text used for fitting/scoring.
method.evidence: Ten automatically chosen quotes per topic at most, contiguous in original extracted source; not representative.
method.validity: Topics describe lexical similarity, not independent stances, verified topic proportions or consensus.

illustrative_quotes.quote: 20554 The Critical Imperative of Sustained E-Rate Funding for K-12 Educational Infrastructure An Articulated Assessment of Category 1 & Category 2 Support on Campus Operations, Instructional Equity, and Long-Term Budgetary Sustainability Executive Summary:  Universal Service E-Rate funding is not an optional technology grant; it is the non-negotiable financial foundation that keeps our public school district connected.

E-RATE SUPPORT FOR RELIABLE INTERNET ACROSS DISTRICT FACILITIES 
E-Rate funding directly powers FCPS’s robust digital architecture through two core funding 
mechanisms: 
● Category 1 (Broadband & WAN Services): Subsidizes high-speed fiber-optic Wide 
Area Network (WAN) connections and internet access across all FCPS schools,
Any reduction or narrowing of E-Rate support would directly compromise network stability, educational continuity, campus safety, and infrastructure reliability.

On behalf of our school district, which serves over 13,000 students
Grace Brocksmith
across ten traditional and virtual schools, I respectfully urge the Federal Communications
Student School
Commission (FCC) to reject any proposal that would sunset, eliminate, reduce, or restrict E-Rate
Board Member
funding for public school districts.
Our district relies heavily on E-Rate funding to cover high-speed internet and replace aging internal network infrastructure, including our local area network switches and wireless access points.

Specifically, these funds provide high-speed fiber internet connectivity, campus-wide wireless access points, and essential 
core network infrastructure, including switches and routers.

From 2014 through 2026, Category 2 investments yielded significant network modernization across our buildings: Cumulative Category 2 Total Cost (USAC + District):  $3,040,047.13 Federal E-Rate Committed Share (85% Discount):  $2,584,040.06 District Cumulative Out-of-Pocket Share (15% Match):  $456,007.07 Our current enterprise network deployment includes approximately  300 Cisco switches  and  750 Meraki wireless access points .

Preserving Digital Equity in Rural Communities As a small, rural district, Knappa relies on E-Rate discounts to maintain essential Category 1 (broadband connectivity) and Category 2 (internal network infrastructure, Wi-Fi, and routing hardware) services.
Our IP security cameras, electronic door key fobs, automated visitor check-in, and emergency notification systems all run directly over the network E-Rate helps fund.

I respectfully urge the Commission to: Reject any proposal to sunset, phase out, or eliminate the E-Rate program; Modernize program bandwidth targets to ensure funding formulas recognize a modern baseline of 1 Gbps with headroom scalable to 10 Gbps; Preserve robust support for both Category 1 connectivity and Category 2 internal infrastructure so small schools can route high-speed capacity directly to student devices; Reject restrictive eligibility rules or arbitrary geographical formulas that penalize small and rural communities; and Work collaboratively with school technology leaders to strengthen and streamline E-Rate rather than dismantle it.

Every applicant pays part of the cost of every service it buys, 
and the Commission’s rules bar service providers from rebating that share.15 Discounts range 
from 20 to 90 percent, and category two discounts stop at 85 percent.16 In funding year 2026, 
applicants filed requests for $4.68 billion in services and sought $3.62 billion in discounts; their 
own share was $1.06 billion.17 An applicant that pays part of every bill buys what it needs and 
sets priorities within its budget.

The NPRM asked stakeholders whether the E-Rate program has already fulfilled the 
requirements prescribed by Congress in section 254, and if so, whether the FCC has authority to 
sunset the E-Rate program.4  The Commission also questioned whether all current eligible 
services supported by E-Rate are necessary and whether the amount of support should be 
reduced, either by narrowing the scope of eligible services, reducing the discount percentage for 
certain schools and libraries, or excluding them altogether.5  The answers to these questions is 
that the E-Rate program continues to be vitally important to all schools and libraries, and the 
amount of support for the current scope of eligible services is essential and should not be 
reduced.

The Commission’s extant rules for consultants, applicants, and 
Service Providers have produced an E-Rate program that reports robust metrics on integrity; we 
welcome reforms meant to drive enhanced integrity while ensuring the E-Rate program remains 
accessible for applicants and eligible institutions.

Q14	14	An ex parte filing by former FCC Commissioner Harold Furchtgott-Roth argues that the E-Rate program, as currently administered, departs from what section 254(h)(1)(B) of the Communications Act authorizes… [See paragraph 14] … We seek comment on each of these points, and on the extent to which the expansion of eligible services and equipment over time to include items beyond discountedtelecommunications services is supported by the text, structure, and history of section 254 of the Communications Act.

The proposed annual 
consultant certification form would be modeled after the current SPAC Form (Form 473), 
requiring consultants to certify knowledge of and compliance with the Commission’s E-Rate 
program rules, conflict of interest rules, and those rules adopted through this proceeding.51  
Under the rules, the Commission would require applicants and service providers to submit 
certification forms completed by all consultants they retain or a certification that they did not use 
a consultant.52  To avoid creating duplicative certification obligations and ease the administrative 
burden on the applicants and service providers responsible for submitting the forms, the 
Commission should ensure the substantive and procedural requirements for the consultant 
certification align with those of existing E-Rate certifications.

Section 254(h)(1)(B) of the Communications Act of 1934, as amended, (Communications 
Act) provides that discounts be applied to services provided to eligible schools and libraries for 
“educational purposes.”4  As a result, the E-Rate program rules require schools and libraries to use 
eligible services “primarily for educational purposes.”5  In the case of schools, “educational purposes” is

The Commission seeks comment on 
whether section 254(h) requires only “that a telecommunications carrier extend a discount to an 
eligible school or library and then recoup it as an offset to its universal service contribution or as 
reimbursement from the support mechanism—not that the fund make payments directly to 
schools, libraries, and consortia, which is one of two invoicing methods currently allowed under 
program rules.”48  Because there is no ETC limitation in section 254(h), the Commission has the 
discretion to allow E-Rate support to be paid directly to school and library applicants through the

Section 254(h)(1)(B) of the Communications Act of 1934, as amended, (Communications 
Act) provides that E-Rate discounts be applied to services provided to eligible schools and libraries for 
“educational purposes.”4  As a result, the E-Rate rules require schools and libraries to use eligible services 
“primarily for educational purposes.”5  In the case of schools, “educational purposes” is defined as 
“activities that are integral, immediate, and proximate to the education of students.”6  In the case of 
libraries, “educational purposes” is defined as activities that are “integral, immediate, and proximate to 
the provision of library services to library patrons.”7
